THE SYSTEM CASEITLE
The system case comprises the chassis (or structural framework) and the enclosure (or covers). It's the metal and plastic box that houses the main components of the computer.
DISCUSSION

Structure is critically important to the proper functioning of the system. The chassis provides a solid framework for mounting the internal components, ensuring that everything fits securely. Without a solid structure to hold things in place, electrical interconnections between components would not be reliable...
The motherboard and power supply both mount directly to the chassis. All the other internal components mount to either the motherboard or the chassis itself, or both.

Protection: The covers provide another critically important function. They protect the inside of the system from outside elements. They protect it from physical damage, foreign objects and liquids which could cause short circuits, and electrical interference..

Cooling: This is the third critically important function of the case. Components that run cooler last longer and give less trouble. A spacious, well laid-out case is as critical to proper system cooling as a good fan..

Smaller cases, such as slimline cases and mini-towers require components to be packed more closely together, which can create cooling problems. Larger cases, such as full towers, provide the most internal space and allow the best air circulation...

Organization and expandability: A case that is sufficiently large and well laid out will make it easier to install and remove expansion cards and drives. If the case is too small, or poorly designed, your upgrade or expansion capability will be limited.............

Expansion cards normally fit into expansion slots, which are card edge connectors located on the motherboard. Most expansion cards are also fastened to the rear panel of the chassis to make sure that they stay securely seated in the connector...

Disk drives are installed into expansion bays, which are mounting brackets rigidly attached to the chassis. Bays may be external, which means that they are visible and accessible from the outside, or they may be internal, which means that they are hidden entirely within the system case...

Status Display: The case usually contains indicator lights that give the user information about what is going on inside the box (not a lot, but some). These may be built into the case or may be part of the devices that are mounted into the case..

Aesthetics: The system case is what people see when they look at the computer. For some people, this isn't important at all; for others, it's essential that their machine looks good, or at least fits somewhat into their d
range in type from desktop cases to massive server towers, but their basic functions are the same. Some types of cases currently available are:

The mini tower is a compact, small footprint design that is easily positioned either on top of a computer desk or on the floor, beside or under the desk. The main disadvantage is that its small interior size limits expandability...
DEFINITION
The mid tower is an excellent overall design that offers similar benefits to the mini tower, but with improved expandability potential.

The full tower allows the widest range of expansion options and the best air circulation for cooling, but it is rather large. You may not be able to place a full tower case on top of, or under, the computer desk. It often ends up standing next to the desk...

The desktop case was not designed for floor use, but some manufacturers make stands that will allow it to be turned on its side. Some desktop cases are strong enough to support the weight of a small monitor, making more efficient use of available desk space...

1. The case provides protection for the internal components. It prevents them from being damaged by foreign objects, helps to shelter them from liquid spills, and shields them from electromagnetic interference...

2. The chassis of the system case provides the structure on which the computer is built. It holds the motherboard and power supply in place; all other internal components mount either to the chassis or to the motherboard or both..

3. The layout of the interior affects the circulation of air which provides the cooling for the internal components. The more spacious and better organized the interior, the better the circulation and therefore the cooler the components......
4. The system case also provides the mounting for the status display indicators and bays for organizing and housing expansion components such as disk drives, while keeping aesthetics in mind.

POWER SUPPLY FORM & FUNCTIONON

The power supply is responsible for converting the 115 VAC source power into the DC voltages that the computer needs. It's called the power supply because it supplies the power for every device within the computer, and sometimes external devices as well...
DISCUSSION
How important is the quality of power supplied to your PC? This chart shows just how important it can be.

These charts show vividly why the power supply is so important. Despite the low cost compared to other PC components, power and cooling (the two primary jobs of the power supply) are responsible for a large percentage of overall system problems....
The power supply also plays an important role in the following areas of your system.

Stability: A high quality power supply-with sufficient capacity to meet the demands of the computer-will provide years of stable power. A poor quality or overloaded power supply will cause a variety of problems..
Cooling: The power supply fan is the primary source of airflow through the PC case. Although some system cases include a supplemental fan, many do not.
Energy Efficiency: Newer power supplies work with the computer's components and software to reduce the amount of power they consume when idle.
Expandability: The capacity of the power supply is an important factor in determining how much a system can be expanded or upgraded.
Power supplies are rated in terms of the number of watts they produce. The higher its wattage, the more power it can provide to the rest of the computer's components.
The main function of the power supply is simple: it converts the 115 VAC source voltage into the DC voltages needed by the computer's various components.

However, the power supply's job isn't as simple as that of a standard power converter. In addition to providing several different voltages at once, the power supply must also manage some additional signals that are used by the motherboard...

PCs use a type of power supply called a switching power supply. Essentially, the switching power supply uses a transistor switch and oscillator with a small transformer instead of just a single, massive transformer to produce its properly regulated DC output...

The disadvantage of a switching power supply is that it must have a load on it in order to operate properly. Applying power with no load attached can damage the power supply. The advantages are that it is small, light, and fairly energy efficient...

Note the voltage sense line and circuit, which act as a closed feedback loop to control the DC output. This feedback loop increases the output as demand increases, and decreases it as load is reduced...
A linear power supply has the advantage of being able to have power applied to it with no load attached, without being damaged. If no power is being drawn, it simply stays inert.

The disadvantages, compared to a switching supply, are that it's larger, requires a more massive transformer, and is inefficient. This inefficiency results in quite a lot of heat being produced, and inside a computer, Heat Is The Enemy...
Next, let's look at power supply form factors..............

The form factor refers to its general shape, dimensions (length, width, height), and the number and type of connectors it provides for the motherboard and disk drives. The form factor of the power supply must match both the system case and the motherboard that it will power...
XT Form Factor - The original IBM PC and its hard-drive equipped successor, the IBM PC/XT, used the same form factor. The power supply was turned on and off via an integral up/down toggle switch...

While the PC/XT power supply began as an IBM design, the company's decision to keep the PC architecture open allowed clone manufacturers to make similar PC boxes and use the same size and shape power supply...

In this manner, the first PC form factor standard was born. It was equipped with a very low-powered supply by today's standards (63.5 watts). The XT added the first PC hard disk drive and doubled the power supply rating to 130 watts, still relatively small by today's standards...

AT Form Factor - In 1984, IBM introduced the IBM PC/AT. Very similar in overall physical design to the PC and XT models that preceded it, the power supply in these units was increased in size and changed slightly in shape, establishing it as a distinct form factor...
Whereas clone manufacturers made a few PC/XT units compatible with the IBM PC and XT, it was with the AT that the PC world really began to explode.
The original AT power supply provided 192 watts, a respectable figure for the time. This represented a tripling of the original PC's power supply output.
It is used in AT form factor cases and with AT or Baby AT form factor motherboards. It uses the same motherboard and drive connectors as the PC/XT form factor.

The AT form factor was the first to introduce tower-style system cases to the PC world. The desktop power supply and tower power supply were internally the same. Only the on/off switch was different...
For the tower case, the switch is on the end of a cable so that the power supply can be located elsewhere within the tower.

The Baby AT form factor is a smaller version of the original AT form factor. Since it is similar but smaller, the Baby AT power supply will fit both the Baby AT form factor cases and the full-size AT cases, in both tower and desktop styles...
Due to this flexibility, which was introduced around the time that PCs began to really grow in popularity, the Baby AT form factor reigned as the most popular design for over a decade.
The Baby AT power supply was made in both a tower and desktop configuration. As in the full-sized AT, they differ only in the type of power switch used.

This form factor was later replaced by the ATX and other form factors. However, the huge installed base of Baby ATs has given manufacturers of new components incentive to provide upgrade options for the millions who still use these systems...
One power supply form factor that has given the Baby AT competition since its inception has been the LPX (Low Profile) form factor.
They are also often called slimline power supplies because LPX cases are often called slimline cases. The main goal of this form factor is size reduction.
ATX Form Factor - At the time of its introduction by Intel in 1995, the ATX was the most significant change in system design since the invention of the PC over a decade earlier.
Although it took several years to catch on, the ATX form factor and its variants became the standard in a large segment of the marketplace.

On the outside, the ATX power supply appears nearly identical to the LPX power supply except that the ATX lacks the AC power pass-through. On the inside, it's different from previous market standards (the Baby AT and LPX form factors) in several important ways...
A True Standard: The ATX form factor is actually a published standard, as opposed to the informal agreements which were previously in place.
+3.3V Power: ATX systems were the first to include +3.3V power directly, avoiding the need for voltage regulators on the motherboard.

Soft Power: ATX systems introduced the +5V Standby and Power On signals. These signals, along with a change to the way the power switch works, make up what is called the Soft Power feature. It enables such things as allowing the operating system to turn the PC on and off..
Additional Signals: ATX defines several additional signals used for fan control, compatibility with newer peripherals, and more.
Changed Motherboard Connectors: Breaking with 15 years of tradition created by the PC/XT, AT, Baby AT and LPX form factors, the ATX and later form factors specify new motherboard connectors...
Where the older form factors used a pair of 6-pin connectors, the ATX uses a single 20-pin connector. This is described more fully, later in the lesson.
Modified Fan Direction and Placement: One of the goals of the original ATX specification was to change the way the power supply fan worked.
Instead of exhausting air out the back of the case, Intel wanted to use this exhaust air to cool the processor directly, saving the cost of a cooling fan.

Unfortunately, while a good idea, this hasn't worked out quite the way they had hoped. The primary problem is that newer CPUs continue to generate more and more heat as they get faster, and a regular power supply fan doesn't provide enough flow to cool them properly...

This problem is compounded by the fact that the air blowing on the CPU is warmed by the components in the power supply, so it is several degrees above ambient temperature before it ever gets near the CPU...

The ATX standard has gone back to the old style of placing the fan on the back of the power supply and exhausting air to the outside. Since it has become the industry standard, ATX power supplies are very common...

SFX Form Factor - In 1997 Intel introduced the new MicroATX motherboard form factor, based upon the original ATX form factor. In 1999 they also produced the FlexATX addendum to the MicroATX specification, detailing plans for an even smaller motherboard and case standard...
Neither the FlexATX nor the MicroATX form factors included specifications for a power supply. Instead, Intel created the SFX power supply form factor.
In many ways the SFX form factor could be considered a little brother to ATX. It is mostly interchangeable with the ATX power supply, but it does not provide the -5 V required for ISA compatibility..

ISA COMPATIBILITY - ISA (Industry Standard Architecture) is an older expansion form. The ISA standard required -5 V to support its expansion cards, but neither MicroATX or FlexATX ISA includes any ISA slots. Since they don't support the standard, the -5 V is no longer relevant.
DEFINITION
Another issue with ATX exchangeability is that an SFX power supply is equipped only with the standard 60 mm fan, which may cause trouble with cooling for a large ATX system case.

WTX Form Factor - Introduced by Intel in 1998 and revised in 1999, the WTX form factor is designed specifically for the larger workstations (thus the W in WTX). It produces all the same voltages as the ATX, and also has some unique signals of its own...

To meet the increased needs of the largest regular PC systems, the WTX form factor is totally different from the other PC form factors. It is designed in a modular way from the ground up to allow it to meet the needs of large, multiple-CPU systems of the present and the future...

The system is segmented physically into different zones where different functions can be incorporated into the system. The power supply has been completely changed to suit the needs of these larger systems...

POWER SUPPLY OUTPUTS & SPECIFICATIONSNSSS
PCs use several different voltages to power their various components. The power supply provides each of these voltages, in varying amounts depending on the model.
DISCUSSION

Most of the power provided by the power supply is in the form of positive DC voltages, but some is in the form of negative DC voltages. Note that whether they are positive or negative, all the outputs are DC...

This chart is an illustration of the various voltages provided by a typical AT power supply. The colors listed correspond to the colors normally used for wires carrying the voltage in the supply's motherboard connectors...
The wires going to peripherals such as disk drives use the same colors but only supply +5 V, +12 V, and Ground.
This chart shows ATX style power supply connections........

PS-ON# (Power Supply Remote On/Off Control)
The maximum amount of current which the power supply can provide at each voltage level is important because it determines the supply's ability to provide sufficient power for your system.
Next, let's briefly discuss each of the various voltages provided by power supplies.

-12V: This voltage is used on the type of serial port circuit whose amplifier circuit requires both -12V and +12V. Newer systems use either +5 V or +3.3 V, but the older style serial ports are still fairly common.

-5 V: A now-archaic voltage, -5 V was used on some of the earliest PCs for floppy disk controllers and was also used by some older ISA bus cards. Although very rarely used by anything anymore, it is still part of the ISA standard and is available for compatibility reasons.
Ground: Also called common or (especially in the UK) earth.
+5 V: On older form factor systems (Baby AT and earlier), this voltage was used to run the motherboard, the CPU (directly or indirectly), and the vast majority of other components in the system...
+12 V: This voltage is used primarily to power disk drive motors and cooling fans.
Power Good signal: When the power supply first starts up, it takes some time for the components to ramp up and start producing the proper DC voltages that the computer needs to operate..
To prevent the computer from starting up prematurely, the power supply sends a signal to the motherboard called Power Good (or PG, or Power OK, etc.).
On older form factor systems (Baby AT and earlier), Power Good was a +5 V signal, but was completely separate from the +5 V operating voltages.
Until the Power Good signal is sent, the motherboard will refuse to start up the computer. Also, the power supply will turn the signal off if a power surge or glitch causes it to malfunction.
Newer systems use a different kind of motherboard connector and have additional signals that were not used on previous systems.

Starting with the second generation Pentium chips, Intel reduced the CPU operating voltage to +3.3 V in order to reduce power consumption as the chips got faster. This required motherboard manufacturers to put voltage regulators on their boards to change the +5 V to +3.3 V.
+3.3 V: This voltage output was introduced with the ATX form factor and is now found on the ATX/NLX, SFX, and WTX form factors.
Soft Power (Power On and 5V Standby Signals): Newer form factors, starting with the ATX/NLX, and including the SFX and WTX, have changed the way the power supply is turned on and off..
Early PCs using the PC/XT, AT, Baby AT and LPX form factors all use a mechanical switch to turn the computer on and off.

In tower cases and some desktop cases, the mechanical switch is not mounted directly to the power supply's chassis. Instead, it is mounted on the end of a cable going to the front panel. Even though it's remotely mounted, it's still hard-wired directly to the power supply...

Instead of using a hard-wired physical switch, ATX and newer systems are turned on by the Soft Power feature which tells the power supply what to do. The signal that controls the power supply is called Power On or PS On...
How can the motherboard electronically tell the power supply to turn on, when the motherboard is also off due to not having any power from the supply?

The answer is the other soft power signal (+5 V Standby, +5 VSB, or 5 VSB). This signal is at the same output level as the regular +5 V lines. However, it is independent of them and is always on while the machine is plugged in, even when the machine itself is turned off.
It is a small amount of current from this wire that allows the motherboard to control the power supply when it is off and permits other activities that must occur while the PC is off.
These other activities include such things as enabling wakeup from sleep mode or allowing the PC to be turned on when activity is detected on a modem (Wake On Ring) or network card (Wake On LAN)...

Generally, ATX-type power supplies of more than 250 watts use an auxiliary six-pin Molex (r) type connector to supply the additional +5 V and +3.3 V to the motherboard. This table shows the color code and pinout used.

The following additional signals are also specified for ATX/NLX systems. They are supplied via another six-pin connector (two rows of three pins each). This table shows the color code and pinout used for these optional signals...
+ 5V DC DC DCV DC5V DC

+3.3 V Sense: This signal is used to detect the voltage level of the +3.3 V signal being provided to the motherboard. It allows the power supply to fine tune the +3.3 V output in the event of excessive voltage drop between the supply and the components that use +3.3 V.
FanC: This is a fan control signal, which allows the motherboard (and hence the system as a whole) to control the speed of the power supply fan..
FanM: A companion to FanC, this is the fan monitor signal, which allows the motherboard to keep track of the speed of the power supply fan.
1394V and 1394R: This pair of signals provides a separate, unregulated voltage circuit for powering IEEE-1394 (FireWire) peripherals. It is not used by the motherboard.
1394V and 1394R: This pair of signals provides a separate, unregulated voltage circuit for powering IEEE-1394 (FireWire) peripherals. It is not used by the motherboard.
DEFINITION
IEEE-1394 (FireWire) - Firewire is an ultra-high-speed file transfer protocol. It is discussed in more detail in a later lesson.
The SFX form factor defines just one optional signal, called Fan ON/OFF, which is essentially the same as the FanC ATX signal described earlier.

WTX, reflecting its status as a high-end form factor, includes all the same voltages plus several additional signals. These include the +3.3 V Sense, FanC, and FanM signals as just described for ATX/NLX, as well as Sleep, +3.3 V AUX, and +5 V Sense.
Sleep: Puts the power supply into sleep mode. This is used for power savings, to power down parts of the power supply.
+3.3 V AUX: This is a standby +3.3 V signal just like the +5 V Standby signal defined for standard ATX Soft Power.
+5 V Sense: Just like the +3.3 V Sense signal, but for +5 V. The WTX form factor also provides special, dedicated grounds (called returns) for its sense lines.

This next section provides a detailed look at the various specifications that accompany power supplies. These specifications are sorted into groups to make them easier to understand. You'll find similar groupings on many manufacturers' specification sheets...
The physical specifications describe how the power supply is physically situated and what the characteristics of its physical pieces are.
Form Factor: Occasionally listed as that of the case in which it normally fits. The most common instance would be a microATX power supply.
Dimensions: The physical dimensions of the case. Normally these are specified as W (width) x D (depth) x H (height). May be given in inches (in or ) or millimeters (mm).
Weight: The weight of the power supply, in pounds (lb) or kilograms (kg).
Motherboard Connectors: The number and type of connectors used to interface the power supply to the motherboard.
Drive Connectors: The number of drive connectors provided as standard equipment with the power supply. Higher-wattage supplies usually provide more connectors.
Fan Characteristics-Size: Size of the power supply fan, usually given in mm. Fans are normally square, and this is the nominal length of one side of the fan.
Fan Characteristics-Bearing Type: Whether the fan's motor uses sleeve or ball bearings.
Fan Characteristics-Voltage: The voltage used to power the fan. If not specified, the default (+12 V) applies.

Fan Characteristics-Capacity: How much air the fan can move, usually specified in CFM (cubic feet per minute). Larger numbers mean that the fan has more cooling power. This is the single most important characteristic of a fan..
Environmental specifications refer to the ambient conditions that the power supply requires in order to function properly.
Operating Temperature Range: The minimum and maximum acceptable ambient temperatures for the power supply while it is operating.
Storage Temperature Range: The minimum and maximum acceptable temperatures for the unit when in storage.

Humidity Range: Acceptable humidity range for operation of the power supply. A typical specification might be 10% to 90% RH where the abbreviation RH stands for relative humidity. Excessive humidity may result in condensation, which can destroy computer equipment..
Altitude Range: Some manufacturers specify a range of acceptable altitudes for use of the equipment.
Input specifications refer to what the power supply requires for its electrical power input. Electrical input specifications are normally provided as a range.
Input Voltage Range: Acceptable input voltages, usually shown as a range of numbers. For example: 85 to 135 V AC or 170 to 270 V AC.
Frequency: Acceptable nominal frequency of input power
(50 Hz or 60 Hz), or alternately, a range of acceptable frequencies (for example, 48-62 Hz). Most power supplies can handle both
Power Factor: The power factor that the power supply presents as a load to the utility power line. Normal power supplies will be in the 60% to 70% range (0.6 to 0.7).
The most important power supply specifications are those that relate to its output levels, since providing those outputs is its purpose.

Output Rating (Watts): The nominal, total maximum output of the power supply in watts. This is actually sometimes not even supplied in the specification sheet; the name of the power supply will usually have a number in it that is supposed to represent this value..
Output Current Rating (Maximum Load By Voltage): The maximum amount of current provided by the power supply at each voltage level.

Minimum Current Rating (Minimum Load Requirement By Voltage): The minimum amount of current that must be drawn by loads within the PC, for each voltage level it provides, in order for it to function properly...

+3.3 V / +5 V Combination Maximum: The maximum amount of total power, in watts, that the power supply can provide simultaneously for the combination of the +3.3 V and +5 V signals. This is an upper limit that constrains any maximum load levels for either of the signals individually.
Peak Output: The amount of current that the voltage specified can supply for a limited amount of time. Usually this is specified only for the +12 V signal.
Output Voltage Range: For each output voltage, the range (tolerances) within which the power supply will operate.

Efficiency: Typical PC power supplies are 60% to 85% efficient. This means that 15% to 40% of the input power is wasted as heat, which must be removed from the machine. Clearly, the more efficient the power supply, the better. A power supply which runs cooler also runs more reliably..
Power Good Delay: The typical time from the moment that power is applied until the Power Good signal is asserted. The manufacturer may also specify a minimum and maximum time.
Auto Restart: some power supplies will automatically restart the system after an AC power failure. If this feature is available, it will be mentioned in the specifications.

Hold Time: The amount of time the power supply will keep producing its output after losing its input. Sometimes called Hold-up Time.

Load Regulation: The ability of the power supply to control the output voltage level as the load on the power supply changes. The voltage of a DC power source tends to decrease as its load increases, and increase as the load decreases..

Line Regulation: Describes the ability of the power supply to control its output levels as the level of the AC input voltage varies from minimum to maximum acceptable level. Values are usually specified as a percentage, with

Ripple: Sometimes called AC Ripple or simply Noise. It results from imperfect filtering of the DC outputs. There will always be some ripple, but less is better. Values are usually given in millivolts peak-to-peak (mVpp)...
Transient Response: A measure of how quickly and effectively the power supply can adjust to sudden changes in load.
Peak Inrush Current / Input Surge Current: The absolute maximum amount of current that the power supply will draw in the moment after it is initially turned on. Lower values are better.
Over-voltage Protection: In addition to specifying a normal maximum voltage level, good power supplies will include protection against the output voltage exceeding a certain critical level...

Over-current Protection: If outputs exceed their maximum ratings, some power supplies will detect this condition and reset the unit. The supply will specify what percentage over the maximum rating will cause this to occur..
There are some power supply specifications that don't pertain specifically to its operation. However, they are important as an indication of the power supply's general quality level.
MTBF/MTTF

Noise Level: Normally rated in dB (decibels). The larger this number, the more noise the power supply causes. As the only component with moving parts, the noise level is determined by the power supply fan(s) ..
MTBF/MTTF

MTBF / MTTF: Mean Time Between Failures/Mean Time To Failure. These figures are an estimate of the number of hours that this type of power supply will run, statistically, before failing. Typical values for power supplies are 30,000 to 50,000 hours and up..
MTBF/MTTF
Warranty: This is the term, in months or years, during which the manufacturer will agree to repair or replace the power supply if it fails.
MTBF/MTTF
Virtually all power supplies have their safety and quality certified by one or more agencies. These certifications indicate that the power supply has been tested and has met a certain standard.
Underwriters Laboratories (UL) is the largest such agency in North America, followed by CSA International (formerly the Canadian Standards Association).

In Europe the majority of certifications are done by NEMKO in Norway, and by TUV and VDE in Germany. Throughout the European Economic Community, the CE mark indicates that the item has met the standards required for items sold within the European Community...

EMI/RFI compliance rules are established in the United States by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). You will see many companies advertise that their power supplies are FCC Class B certified...

Finally, some power supplies are Energy Star certified. This is an EPA program established to help promote energy-efficient PCs and components. Modern form factor specifications will detail the requirements for the power supply to achieve Energy Star compliance...

The lack of certification of a device does not mean necessarily that it is a bad product. It simply means that the product hasn't been thoroughly tested to meet the regular standards in the industry...
This concludes the discussion of POWER SUPPLY OUTPUTS AND SPECIFICATIONS.
1. Starting with the second generation Pentium chips, the CPU operating voltage was reduced to +3.3 V in order to reduce power consumption.
2. A +3.3 V output was introduced with the ATX form factor and is now found on the ATX/NLX, SFX, and WTX form factors....

3. -5 V was used on some of the earliest PCs for floppy disk controllers and was also used by some older ISA bus cards. It is still part of the ISA standard and is available for compatibility reasons, but is not otherwise used.

4. WTX includes several additional signals besides those specified for ATX. These include Sleep, +3.3 V AUX, and +5 V Sense. It also provides special, dedicated grounds (called returns) for its sense lines.
5. The wires going to peripherals such as disk drives use red, yellow, and black to supply +5 V, +12 V, and Ground, respectively.
6. +12 V is used primarily to power disk drive motors and cooling fans..
7. Hold (or Hold-up) Time is the amount of time the power supply will keep producing its output after losing its input.
8. The Power Good signal prevents the computer from starting up before the power supply has had a chance to ramp up to full output and stabilize.
9. The physical specifications describe how the power supply is physically situated and what the characteristics of its physical pieces are.

10. ATX-type power supplies of more than 250 watts usually use an auxiliary six-pin connector to supply the additional +5 V and +3.3 V to the motherboard. Another six-pin connector supplies fan control signals, +3.3 V sense, and IEEE-1394 (firewire) power.
